. He played it on the floor like that and stuff. George had people stand on his chest. Yeah, jump on his chest. What we call that eccentric. So Henry did all that too. Henry done that before George did that. Yeah, sure. Henry was really the originator of it. Well, uh, start. I didn't get that on here. You say Henry could read a good reader, but the rest of you never did learn to read. No, none of us read outside of Henry. Henry would sit down and play first chair in a big 60-piece band. And he could tell you if any instrument was out of tune. Did you have any teacher and mostly learn to pick up the trombone yourself? No. You first played, of course, other instruments. You played several of them. How many have the trombone and the trumpet, or did you play anything else? Alto, baritone? No, I played alto. I played a baritone. I played sousaphone and trombone and trumpet. You learned all those yourself then? Yeah, just picked it up by... You ever played the slide? Yes, I can play a little slide, but I'm a little... Feel more at home on the other. I feel more at home on the other one because I can get more harmony. Yeah. And, uh... You know, when you're playing with a small combination, you've got to get that close harmony, you see?
Who were some of the other fellas you were with in Chicago when you made the records? Well... I don't remember that.

I believe I got them in that scrapbook. Oh, that's real. We'll still find all that. Look it up, sir. I got a picture of my whole band in this scrapbook. Oh, that's good, yeah. But I don't believe the names are in there. Well, we'll check with you. Well, now, my drummer was Bill Paley. Bill Paley, you want to put it down? Yeah, and we'll have it on the tape here anyway. We'll have it, yeah. We've got it on the tape, don't we? Bill Paley was my drummer. Norman Vanhoek was my bass man. Sousaphone. Maury Friedman was my piano man. Uh, Raleigh the Foe. Yeah, I know him. And Willie Krieger was my two clarinets and sax man. And they're both on the record? Yeah. And Franz Piper was my banjo man.

And Gordon Paulyat, when I put a show in there, he was on trombone. And Gordon Paulyat, when I put a show in there, he was on trombone. And I couldn't read and I had to put a show in there. And I had to put a violin player, and a man that doubled on trumpet, so he could carry the lead, see? And I was directing the band.
Who was Lou King by the way?
Well, he was a singer, an entertainer in the place. He used to sing with the entertainers on the floor, and he made a couple of records with us. What about Angry, that tune?
How did that come to the degree of the six? Well, we wrote Angry in Bluxy here.

Jules Kazard, my brother Henry and I, and when I went to Chicago, and when I was in California, my brother George called me and told me he was going to make a record of it. Him and Paul, Paul Mez and George and him, with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, and they made a record of Angry. So then I got busy and got lyrics to it, and I got a man by the name of Dudley Mecham to put lyrics to. Where is he? Is he here? He's in Chicago. Chicago. Chicago. Chicago.

Tiny Hill made a record of it, K-Stars. Where did everybody? There's a lot of left. Lawrence Waltz sings it every now and then. Perry Como had it on his fall show. And I got a man by the name of Dudley Mecham to put lyrics to. Where is he? Is he here? And George called me in Nightfall last and told me that there's a young boy come out with a small combo that made a terrific record of it. And it's a big, big thing in Chicago. So I've been wanting to just like.
Really? Did you get it? Okay.
I guess time to go again, huh? Yeah. Well, we appreciate it. Maybe we'll have a minute after we get through if you don't mind. Yeah, okay. A couple of minutes when we get through. Thanks very much.
Maybe first of all, if you just want to give us your name and maybe when you were born where? Jules Galley. We're going right here in Biloxi. 1903.

segments.title: Abby and Merritt Brunies on family, New Orleans bands, Halfway House, Merritt's career
segments.summary: One long block: Abby's school band and Jack Lane's Reliance Band, the Irish Channel, first jobs, the Halfway House Orchestra, Bucktown and West End; then Merritt's instruments, Chicago bands, police career, and Papa Lane's ragtime band.

segments.title: Henry as eccentric trombonist; none of the brothers read music
segments.summary: Merritt says Henry originated playing trombone with his foot, was the only reader, and that the others picked up their instruments themselves.

segments.title: Merritt's Chicago band personnel and singer Lou King
segments.summary: Merritt names his Chicago drummer, bass, piano, reeds and banjo players, Henry and Gordon Paulyat on trombone, and says Lou King was an entertainer who sang and recorded with them.

segments.title: Writing and recording of 'Angry'
segments.summary: Merritt says 'Angry' was written in Biloxi with Henry, recorded by George with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, then given lyrics and later recorded by Tiny Hill and others.

segments.title: Wrap-up and start of Jules Galley's interview
segments.summary: The Brunies session ends and the interviewer begins a new interview with Jules Galley in Biloxi.
